transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-10-06
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Rossi (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (CISO, Orion Bank), Ethan Cole (Head of Infrastructure), Sofia Ruiz (Compliance Lead), Marcus Lee (Product Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
- Discussed private VPC deployment model and network isolation patterns.
- Confirmed customer-managed KMS requirement and log forwarding to Splunk.
- Agreed next steps to share diagrams and templates; schedule follow-up.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Luca, our solutions engineer. How are you all?
[00:05] Priya: Hi Maya, thanks. This is Priya. We're good, thanks. Busy week.
[00:07] Ethan: Ethan here, hi. Looking forward to the deep dive.
[00:09] Sofia: Sofia on compliance, hi.
[00:10] Marcus: Marcus, product security.
[00:12] Luca: Great to meet you all. quick agenda: we'll run through the private VPC architecture, network boundaries, ingress/egress controls, KMS options, logging, and then Q&A. We'll leave time for specifics.
[00:24] Priya: Sounds good. Our main things up front: we need to validate network isolation, customer-managed keys (we'd prefer BYOK), and also how you handle audit logs and retention — we ship everything to Splunk and need SIEM parity. Also SOC 2 artifacts and pentest cadence.
[00:40] Maya: Absolutely. We'll go step by step. Luca, can you share the high-level diagram?
[00:45] Luca: Yep give me one second — okay I'm sharing my screen, hopefully the diagram is visible. So on the left you can see the control plane which remains in Redwood-managed account but we offer an option for a private control plane in some enterprise packages. The data plane — the inference workers — run in the customer's VPC. We usually recommend dedicated subnets for compute, separate public and private subnets, and a transit VPC / peering model for traffic to central logging.
[01:12] Marcus: Quick question: when you say control plane is Redwood-managed, does that mean customer data ever traverses our account? We have strict audit rules about any egress of PII.
[01:22] Luca: Good question. By default control plane metadata (job state, metrics) goes to Redwood, but payloads can be kept strictly in the data plane. For Private VPC we support a mode where no inference payload leaves the customer's VPC — calls are processed locally. There are two modes: private with redwood control plane (control signals only, telemetry), or fully private where both control and data plane are in customer-managed environment (on-prem or VPC with private control plane). We can support that for regulated workloads.
[01:46] Priya: For regulated data we need the fully private option. Is that GA or coming soon?
[01:50] Maya: It's generally available as an enterprise offering — there are customers on it. We can share reference architecture and the SOC2 + pen test reports.
[01:58] Ethan: Network wise, how do you handle ingress — do we put a load balancer in front of the workers? What about NAT for outbound?
[02:06] Luca: Typically, you put internal ALBs (or NLBs) in private subnets fronting the inference autoscaling groups. Outbound internet access is restricted — we recommend using NAT Gateway or egress via proxy/appliance for updates and model pulls. For tighter control, customers use an egress-only NAT with firewall rules or a transit gateway to route egress through a central inspection appliance (NGFW).
[02:28] Sofia: Will we be able to define strict egress allowlists? We only allow specific endpoints to be contacted for model pulls or OS updates.
[02:33] Luca: Yes, we support allowlists. Model artifacts can be pulled from a customer-controlled S3 or from Redwood's private URIs; if from Redwood URIs, we can do a signed, time-limited transfer or mirror model artifacts into the customer's bucket. That way no dynamic external egress is required during runtime.
[02:51] Marcus: What's the recommended pattern for firewalling? Security groups vs NACLs vs NGFWs?
[02:56] Luca: For host-level controls use security groups with least-privilege rules — allow only the necessary ports between services (e.g., 5000/8080 for inference). NACLs provide subnet-level stateless protection and are good defense-in-depth. For egress inspection and advanced rules, put an NGFW in the egress path or use a managed appliance in a transit VPC. We have templates for security group and NACL configs that customers can import.
[03:18] Maya: I'll attach those templates to the follow-up.
[03:21] Priya: Good. On encryption, we have a hard requirement for customer-managed keys in a FIPS 140-2 HSM. Do you support BYOK with HSM-backed CMKs?
[03:30] Luca: Yes — we support customer-managed KMS keys. For cloud deployments: you can use your KMS (AWS KMS with external key material or CloudHSM) to encrypt model weights at rest and the KV caches. For on-prem we can integrate with on-prem HSMs via PKCS#11 connectors. We also support envelope encryption — Redwood's runtime can accept a CMK to unwrap per-node data keys.
[03:50] Ethan: How does key rotation work? Do you handle re-encryption of cached state?
[03:54] Luca: Rotation is customer-controlled. We provide tooling to rewrap keys and rotate node-level encryption keys with minimal downtime. For large KV caches we do a lazy re-encryption approach (rotate key metadata and re-encrypt on next write) to avoid mass IO. We document the window and guidance for rewrap.
[04:12] Marcus: What about TLS for in-transit? mTLS between control plane and data plane?
[04:16] Luca: All traffic is TLS 1.2+ by default. For stricter needs we support mutual TLS between services and client cert provisioning. In fully private deployments there's an option to disable public endpoints entirely and install certs via your PKI.
[04:30] Sofia: Logging — we need full audit trails to meet our SOC2 and also to feed Splunk. Can logs be forwarded in real time? Are PII redaction tools available?
[04:39] Maya: Yes, logs (audit events, request/response metadata, system logs) can be forwarded to your SIEM — via direct syslog, Kinesis/Firehose, or using an S3 bucket that you own plus a forwarding Lambda. We support configurable log levels and can redact request payloads at the point of egress; i.e., we can truncate or hash sensitive fields before writing.
[05:00] Priya: Important to note: we can't have raw request bodies landing in third-party accounts. We need to ensure that any forwarded logs are scrubbed, and we need a proofing mechanism.
[05:08] Luca: Understood. For deployments where the customer owns the data plane, logs never leave your account unless you configure forwarding. For Redwood-managed control plane, we can configure scrubbing policies and show examples. We also provide log signing for tamper evidence.
[05:24] Ethan: For network monitoring, do you provide VPC flow logs and packet capture hooks?
[05:28] Luca: We recommend enabling VPC Flow Logs and sending them to your log analytics. Packet capture for forensics is something we don't enable by default at scale, but we have tooling to spin short-lived capture instances for incident response.
[05:42] Marcus: What's your pen testing cadence and can we do our own pentest on the deployed infra?
[05:46] Maya: We run annual third-party pentests and can share redacted reports. Customers can run pentests against their VPC deployment; we have a process to pre-authorize scopes and time windows. We ask to validate tests with our security team to avoid accidental service disruption.
[06:01] Sofia: SOC2 — do you have Type II? Can you share the report under NDA?
[06:05] Maya: Yes we have SOC 2 Type II. We'll share the report under standard NDA, plus ISO 27001 summary where available.
[06:11] Priya: Good. Data residency: some of our workloads must remain in EU region and never leave. Is region pinning supported for both model and telemetry?
[06:19] Luca: Yes — you can pin both model artifacts and runtime to a region. Telemetry can be region-restricted or forwarded to your regional SIEM. If you require EU-only isolation, we can provision the whole stack in the EU region with no cross-region replication unless explicitly configured.
[06:34] Ethan: Connectivity options: VPN vs Direct Connect / Interconnect? Latency concerns for inference — we prefer Direct Connect for low latency between our network and Redwood's managed control plane, but if control plane is on-prem that's better.
[06:46] Luca: Many banks use Direct Connect or Interconnect for control plane telemetry. For fully private deployments, the control plane can be deployed to your VPC and you avoid that hop. We'll map the latency requirements and recommend a topology.
[06:58] Priya: About RBAC and SSO — we need SCIM for provisioning and SAML SSO via Okta, and role separation so infra ops can't see request bodies.
[07:08] Luca: We support SAML 2.0 SSO and SCIM provisioning, and role-based access control with tenant-level roles. You can granularly restrict who can view logs vs who can manage deployments. For extra segmentation, we can mask request bodies in logs and restrict them to a compliance-only role.
[07:27] Marcus: Any capabilities for session recording / approval workflows before model rollouts?
[07:31] Maya: We have rollout policies and can gate model promotions behind approvals. We can keep audit trails of who approved a model and when.
[07:38] Ethan: Can we see a sample of the security groups and NACL templates?
[07:41] Luca: Yes — I'll attach them. They include recommended port lists, least-privileged egress lists, and NGFW rules for transit.
[07:48] Priya: A few edge cases: what about CVE responses on the inference runtime? We need patch SLAs and hotfix windows.
[07:56] Luca: We publish a security bulletin and have patching policies. For fully managed nodes we apply critical patches within 48 hours, non-critical per maintenance windows agreed with customers. In private deployments we can give you the patch schedule and allow you to opt into managed patching or self-managed.
[08:14] Sofia: For compliance evidence, besides SOC2, we need continuous monitoring proofs — how long do you retain audit logs and can retention be configured per customer?
[08:22] Luca: Retention is configurable. By default we retain system audit logs for 90 days in the managed offering; enterprise customers can configure longer retention and export to cold storage (S3) under their account for 7+ years.
[08:35] Priya: Great. Regarding egress filtering: can we enforce egress through our proxies and inspect TLS? TLS interception is sensitive but we have an internal TLS inspection appliance for enterprise traffic.
[08:46] Luca: You can route egress through your inspection appliance. We recommend preserving end-to-end TLS for payloads; interception is only for metadata and outbound updates. If you require TLS inspection we can sign certs with your internal CA in the private deployment.
[09:00] Marcus: Any limitations on model size or KV cache that affect encryption or network?
[09:04] Luca: Model size mostly affects storage and startup time. Large models will pull artifacts at deployment time — recommended to pre-stage in your bucket. KV cache is local to nodes; encryption overhead is small. We document perf numbers for typical model families.
[09:17] Maya: Okay we're getting to time. Quick recap: Maya will share SOC2 and architecture diagrams; Luca will produce SG/NACL templates and checklist; Priya/Ethan will confirm compliance list and network contacts.
[09:29] Priya: Perfect. One last question — do you support air-gapped on-prem deployment?
[09:33] Luca: Yes, we have an on-prem package for air-gapped envs. It includes an installer and options for offline model loading via physical media, and for entirely private control plane. We have docs and a reference engagement.
[09:45] Ethan: Good to know.
[09:47] Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the assets and set the follow-up. Appreciate your time.
[09:52] Marcus: Thanks.
[09:54] Sofia: Thanks all.

End of transcript
